questions.prompt: What does it mean that Apex is a 'strongly typed' language?
options: Every variable must have an explicit declared type, checked by the compiler before the code runs
Apex automatically converts any value to any type with no restrictions
Only sObject variables require a declared type
Type checking happens only at runtime, never at compile time
questions.explain: Strong typing means every variable's type is fixed at declaration and verified by the compiler, rejecting mismatches before the code ever executes.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a loosely/dynamically typed language, the opposite of what Apex actually is. Apex requires explicit types and rejects mismatches at compile time, rather than silently converting between types.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ member belongs to the class itself, with one shared copy across every instance, and must be accessed through the class name rather than through an object reference.
questions.explain: A static member belongs to the class itself rather than to any one object — all instances share a single copy, and it must be referenced through the class name, e.g. RunTracker.totalRuns.

questions.prompt: Match each Apex collection type to its defining behavior.
right: A fixed, named set of possible values, checked at compile time
An ordered collection, indexed from 0, that allows duplicate elements
Key-value pairs where each unique key maps to exactly one value
An unordered collection with no duplicate elements
questions.explain: A List is ordered and index-based and allows duplicates. A Set is unordered with no duplicates, useful for membership checks. A Map holds key-value pairs for fast lookup by key. An enum defines a fixed, named set of values checked at compile time, distinct from any collection type.

questions.prompt: What does `obj.write()` print, and what concept does this demonstrate?
options: 'Writing some text using the yellow marker.' — this demonstrates polymorphism, since the actual behavior comes from the subclass even though obj is declared as the parent type
'Writing some text.' — because obj is declared as type Marker, the parent's version always runs regardless of the actual object
A compile error, since YellowMarker cannot be assigned to a variable declared as Marker
Both messages print, one after the other, since override runs both versions
questions.explain: Because obj actually holds a YellowMarker instance, calling write() runs the overridden version even though the variable is declared as the parent type Marker — this is exactly what polymorphism means.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about interfaces and inheritance in Apex, per Chapter 1.
options: A class can implement multiple interfaces at once, comma-separated
A class can extend more than one other class at once
A method in a parent class must be declared virtual before a subclass can override it
An interface's methods have signatures but no bodies, and an implementing class must supply every body
A class that implements an interface automatically inherits a working default implementation for each method
questions.explain: A class can implement several interfaces at once, but Apex allows extending only one class (no multiple inheritance of classes). A method must be virtual to be overridden. Interface methods have no bodies at all, so an implementing class must write every one itself, unlike extending a class, which inherits full implementations for free.

questions.prompt: What is the key behavioral difference between a plain DML statement like `insert accts;` and `Database.insert(accts, false)`?
options: The plain statement is all-or-nothing and throws a DmlException on any failure; Database.insert with allOrNone=false allows partial success and returns per-record results instead of throwing
There is no real difference; both behave identically in every case
Database.insert can only be used on a single record, never a list
The plain DML statement always ignores validation rules, while Database.insert enforces them
questions.explain: Plain DML statements are all-or-nothing, throwing a DmlException if any record fails. Database.insert(records, false) processes each record independently, letting good records commit while failed ones are reported in a Database.SaveResult array instead of throwing.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C is incorrect — Database.insert works on either a single sObject or a List of sObjects, the same as plain DML. The allOrNone parameter, not the input shape, is what distinguishes the two approaches.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ________ DML statement combines up to three duplicate records of the same type into one master record, and is only available for Account, Contact, Case, and Lead.
questions.explain: merge reassigns related child records to the chosen master and deletes the duplicates, but it only works on the four standard objects Account, Contact, Case, and Lead.

questions.prompt: Match each relationship query concept to what it actually describes.
left: Dot notation (e.g. Account.Name on a Contact query)
A subquery in the SELECT list (e.g. (SELECT LastName FROM Contacts))
right: The plural name used to access a parent-to-child subquery's results on the parent record
Used for a custom object's relationship name on both lookups and subqueries
Traversing child-to-parent to read a field from the related parent record
Traversing parent-to-child to pull related child records in the same query
questions.explain: Dot notation reaches child-to-parent for a parent field. A nested subquery reaches parent-to-child for related children. __r is the custom-object relationship suffix used both ways. The child relationship name (like Contacts) is what you use to access the subquery's results on the parent record in Apex.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a savepoint-based partial rollback, per Lesson 17, in the correct order.
items: Attempt one or more DML statements inside a try block
Catch the DmlException thrown by a failing statement
Call Database.rollback(sp) to undo everything back to the savepoint
Continue executing the rest of the transaction using only the data that existed at the savepoint
questions.explain: A savepoint-based rollback runs in this order: mark the checkpoint, attempt the risky DML inside a try block, catch the failure, roll back to the savepoint to undo just that portion of work, and then continue the transaction from that restored state — without ending the whole transaction the way an uncaught exception would.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about exception handling in Apex, per Chapter 2.
options: A custom exception class is created by extending Apex's built-in Exception class
finally always runs, even if a return statement inside try or catch is about to exit the method
catch (Exception e) can never match a DmlException, since DmlException is a completely separate type
If PaymentDeclinedException extends OrderException, a catch (OrderException oe) block also catches a thrown PaymentDeclinedException
Multiple catch blocks for the same try should be ordered from least specific to most specific
questions.explain: Custom exceptions extend Exception. finally always runs before control leaves, even past a pending return. Every built-in and custom exception extends the base Exception class, so catch (Exception e) does match a DmlException. A catch block for a parent exception type also matches any of its subclasses. Catch blocks should be ordered from most specific to least specific, not the reverse, since Apex checks them top to bottom and runs the first match.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the seven Apex trigger events?
options: before undelete
before insert
after update
after undelete
questions.explain: There is no before undelete event — undelete only fires an after event, since there's nothing to validate before a record is restored from the Recycle Bin.
questions.distractorExplain: before insert, after update, and after undelete are all genuine trigger events among the seven (before insert, before update, before delete, after insert, after update, after delete, after undelete) — only before undelete does not exist.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a trigger receives up to ________ records in a single invocation, so a DML operation on 450 records fires the trigger three separate times.
questions.explain: Salesforce processes DML in batches of up to 200 records per trigger invocation, which is why bulkified trigger code must never assume it's only ever handling one record.

questions.prompt: Match each Trigger context variable to the event(s) it is actually available in.
right: True whenever the current Apex code is running in a trigger context at all
Available in before update, after insert, after update, and after undelete
Available on insert, update, and undelete — not available on delete
Available on update and delete — not available on insert
questions.explain: Trigger.new holds current record versions and is unavailable on delete (no new version exists). Trigger.old holds prior versions and is unavailable on insert (no prior version exists). Trigger.newMap is the Id-keyed version of Trigger.new, available in the listed contexts. Trigger.isExecuting is true any time the code is running inside a trigger context at all.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the bulkified query-once pattern from Lesson 23 in the correct order.
items: Loop once over Trigger.new to collect every needed related Id into a Set<Id>
Run a single SOQL query filtering with WHERE Id IN :theSet
Build a Map<Id, SObjectType> keyed by Id from that query's results
Loop again over Trigger.new, looking each related record up in the Map instead of querying
Issue one DML statement on the collected list after the second loop ends
questions.explain: The bulk-safe pattern collects Ids first, queries once with an IN clause, loads the results into an Id-keyed Map for fast lookup, loops a second time using that Map instead of per-record queries, and issues exactly one DML statement at the end — regardless of whether the batch holds 1 or 200 records.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about trigger recursion and the one-trigger-per-object practice, per Chapter 3.
options: An after update trigger that issues an update on the same object can cause itself to fire again
A static Boolean recursion guard works because static variables persist for the duration of one transaction
Salesforce guarantees that OpportunityTrigger1 always runs before OpportunityTrigger2 if both are on the same object and event
A static Set<Id> guard avoids the all-or-nothing limitation of a single shared Boolean flag
Having multiple triggers on the same object and event is recommended, since it keeps each team's logic independent
questions.explain: An after-update trigger's own update can re-fire itself, which is exactly the recursion problem this chapter addresses. A static Boolean guard relies on static variables persisting per transaction. A Set<Id> guard is more precise than an all-or-nothing Boolean, since it tracks specific records rather than blocking all re-entry. Execution order across multiple triggers on the same object and event is explicitly NOT guaranteed, which is exactly why Lesson 22 recommends one trigger per object instead of multiple independent ones.

questions.prompt: Why does Salesforce enforce governor limits on Apex code?
options: Because the Lightning Platform is multi-tenant, and one org's code must not be able to degrade performance for every other org sharing the same infrastructure
Because Apex is an interpreted language and interpreters are always slow
Because governor limits are only a legal requirement in certain countries
Because Salesforce charges extra for code that runs without limits
questions.explain: Salesforce is multi-tenant — many orgs share the same servers — so governor limits exist specifically to stop one org's code from consuming unbounded resources at the expense of everyone else on that infrastructure.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is not the real reason — governor limits exist because of multi-tenancy, not because interpreted languages are inherently slow. Apex's performance characteristics are a separate topic from why hard resource ceilings are enforced at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the documented limit on total SOQL queries issued per synchronous Apex transaction is ________.
questions.explain: Salesforce's Apex Developer Guide documents 100 total SOQL queries per synchronous transaction, with a higher ceiling of 200 for asynchronous transactions.

questions.prompt: Match each Apex sharing keyword to its actual behavior.
right: An indeterminate, caller-dependent behavior Salesforce's own guidance says to avoid
Enforces the running user's sharing rules for that class
Explicitly turns off sharing-rule enforcement for that class
Runs in whatever sharing mode the calling context used, behaving as with sharing at an entry point like a REST service
questions.explain: with sharing enforces the running user's sharing rules. without sharing explicitly disables that enforcement. inherited sharing takes on the caller's sharing mode, acting as with sharing at a true entry point. Leaving the keyword off entirely produces indeterminate, caller-dependent behavior that Salesforce's own guidance treats as an anti-pattern to avoid.

questions.prompt: A developer hardcodes a RecordType Id as a literal string in a trigger, and the code works correctly in the sandbox where it was written. What is the most likely outcome when this code is deployed to production?
options: The code silently misbehaves in production, because record Ids like RecordType Ids are not guaranteed to be the same across sandboxes and production
The code will always behave identically everywhere, since Ids never change between environments
The deployment will fail to compile, since Apex rejects hardcoded Id literals
Salesforce automatically translates the hardcoded Id to the correct production value during deployment
questions.explain: A RecordType Id that is correct in one org's sandbox is very likely different in production, so a hardcoded literal silently points at the wrong (or nonexistent) record in the new environment, with no compile error to warn you.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Custom Metadata Types and Custom Settings, per Lesson 30.
options: Custom Metadata Type records are exempt from the per-transaction SOQL query limit
Custom Metadata Type records are deployable metadata that moves automatically with a deployment or package
Custom Settings data is regular org data that does not travel with a deployment the way Custom Metadata Type records do
Hierarchy Custom Settings cannot resolve differently for different users
getAll() is a generated static method available on both Custom Metadata Types and Custom Settings
questions.explain: Custom Metadata Type records are exempt from the SOQL limit and move with deployments as metadata. Custom Settings data is ordinary org data that must be migrated separately. getAll() is a generated static method on both. Hierarchy Custom Settings specifically CAN resolve to different values per org, profile, or user — that's their entire purpose, so the claim that they can't is false.

questions.prompt: This Opportunity-automation handler checks only `opp.StageName == 'Closed Won'`, without comparing against `oldOpp.StageName`. What real problem does this create?
options: A follow-up Task gets created again on every subsequent update to an Opportunity that was already Closed Won, not just on the actual transition into that stage
The code will fail to compile, since oldMap is declared but never used
No real problem — checking only the new StageName is equivalent to comparing against the old value
The handler will throw a NullPointerException on every single update
questions.explain: Without comparing against the prior StageName, the condition is true on every update to an already-closed-won Opportunity, not just the moment it first transitions — exactly the bug Lesson 33's actual handler avoids by checking oldOpp.StageName != 'Closed Won' too.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of capturing a debug log from a real UI action (not Execute Anonymous), per Lesson 36, in the correct order.
items: Go to Setup → Debug Logs → New Trace Flag
Set the Trace Flag for the specific user and a time window, choosing log levels for relevant categories like Apex_Code and Database
Perform the real UI action (e.g. a button click or record save) that should trigger the Apex code
Open the resulting debug log from the Debug Logs list
Filter the log to USER_DEBUG lines to find your own System.debug() output efficiently
questions.explain: Capturing a log from real UI activity means setting up the Trace Flag first (choosing the user, time window, and log levels), performing the action that should generate the log, then opening and filtering that log to the USER_DEBUG lines rather than reading the whole thing top to bottom.

questions.prompt: Match each data-cleanup scenario to the correct tool, per Lesson 35.
left: A few hundred records need a one-time field fix
80,000 records need a one-time field fix
A query returning more than 50,000 rows
A job that needs to run repeatably, not just once
right: Exceeds the SOQL row limit regardless of code structure — needs Batch Apex's chunked processing
Favors Batch Apex even if the current volume is manageable, since one-time anonymous scripts aren't meant to be rerun
A plain, bulkified anonymous Apex script is simpler and sufficient
Exceeds the DML row limit in one transaction — needs Batch Apex to split the work
questions.explain: Small one-time jobs are well served by a simple bulkified anonymous script. 80,000 records exceeds the 10,000-row DML limit in one transaction, requiring Batch Apex. A 50,000+ row query also requires Batch Apex's chunking, since it exceeds the SOQL row limit. A job meant to run repeatably is better built as Batch Apex from the start rather than as a one-off script.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Apex code review checklist from Lesson 38.
options: A SOQL query or DML statement inside a for loop is a hard rule finding with no legitimate exception
An empty catch (Exception e) {} block is a legitimate way to handle any exception safely
Whether a given piece of automation needs full Selector/Service layering is treated as a reasonable judgment call, not a hard rule
Reviewing a trigger handler should start by confirming it correctly assumes it could receive up to 200 records, not just one
Hardcoded record/RecordType/Profile Ids are specifically called out as something a reviewer should flag
questions.explain: The loop-based query/DML anti-pattern is a hard rule. Selector/Service layering decisions are explicitly framed as judgment calls. Confirming bulk-safety is the first thing to check in a trigger handler review. Hardcoded Ids are explicitly flagged. An empty catch block, however, is called out as a concern precisely because it silently swallows real problems — it is not a legitimate safe handling pattern.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 34, when is using a declarative Case Assignment Rule the better choice over writing an Apex trigger for Case routing?
options: For simple, field-based routing logic that declarative rules can already express through clicks, without needing cross-object lookups or callouts
Never — Apex is always the correct tool for Case routing regardless of complexity
Only when the org has no Apex licenses available
Only for orgs with fewer than 100 total Cases
questions.explain: This lesson is explicit that for simple field-based routing, declarative Case Assignment Rules are genuinely the right tool — Apex earns its place once the routing logic needs something declarative rules can't easily express, such as cross-object lookups or callouts.

questions.prompt: What does the `@RestResource(urlMapping='/ContactService/*')` annotation do?
options: Defines the URL path, relative to the org's REST base, that routes external requests to this class
Marks a method as callable from Flow or Process Builder
Encrypts the class's return value before sending it over HTTP
Declares the class as a trigger handler for the Contact object
questions.explain: The class-level @RestResource annotation defines the URL mapping that external REST callers use to reach this Apex class, relative to /services/apexrest/.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes @InvocableMethod, a completely different annotation used for Flow-callable Apex, not Apex REST services. @RestResource is specifically about exposing a class as a custom REST endpoint.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every numeric value parsed by `JSON.deserializeUntyped()` comes back as a ________, regardless of whether the original JSON number had a decimal point.
questions.explain: JSON.deserializeUntyped() always returns numeric values as Decimal, which is why casting to (Decimal) — and converting further with intValue() if a whole number is specifically needed — is the expected, correct pattern.

questions.prompt: Match each JSON class method to what it actually does.
right: Parses JSON of unknown shape into generic Map/List structures
Converts an Apex object into a compact JSON string
Parses JSON directly into an instance of a known Apex class
Converts an Apex object into an indented, readable JSON string
questions.explain: serialize() produces compact JSON. serializePretty() produces the same data with indentation for readability. deserialize() with a Type.class literal parses into a known class. deserializeUntyped() parses JSON of unknown shape into generic Map/List structures the caller navigates manually.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about enums and @InvocableMethod in Apex, per Chapter 6.
options: An enum variable can only ever be assigned one of its declared values, catching a typo as a compile error rather than a silent runtime bug
@InvocableMethod always takes a List of its input wrapper class and returns a List of its output wrapper class, even for a Flow that only passes one record
Only private or static variables can be marked @InvocableVariable
A single when branch in a switch on statement can match multiple comma-separated values at once
Wrapper classes are a special built-in Apex language feature, distinct from ordinary classes
questions.explain: Enums are checked at compile time, catching typos that a plain String would miss. @InvocableMethod requires the List-in/List-out signature because Flow can call an action with a bulk collection of records. A when branch can list multiple comma-separated values. However, only public or global variables can be marked @InvocableVariable (not private or static), and a wrapper class is just an ordinary class used for a specific bundling purpose, not a distinct language feature.

questions.prompt: Both lines compute the correct answer, but one is a meaningfully better performance choice for a large collection used purely for membership checks. Which, and why?
options: Set.contains() is the better choice, because a List performs a linear scan for contains() while a Set is the structure actually designed for efficient membership checks
List.contains() is the better choice, because Lists are always faster than Sets in Apex
There is no real difference; both execute in exactly the same way internally
Set.contains() is better only because Sets cannot hold duplicate values, which is unrelated to performance
questions.explain: List.contains() scans the list entry by entry (a linear scan), while Set is the collection type specifically designed for efficient membership checks — choosing the right collection for the job, as this course's capstone lesson emphasizes, is itself a performance decision.
